hypothesis: ADR-002's premise that 'runtime detection ≠ prevention' is a false dichotomy that misdiagnoses the real design space: a transaction-scoped check evaluated BEFORE state commits is genuinely preventive, so bloom's runtime view-function invariant (H2) is either (a) preventive already and thus contradicts its own stated limitation, or (b) strictly dominated by carrying a per-transaction proof obligation. Either way the ADR-002 rationale is wrong as written.
rationale: 'Theorem-Carrying Transactions: Runtime Verification to Ensure Interface Specifications for Smart Contract Safety' (2024) demonstrates that a runtime mechanism can be fully PREVENTIVE: every transaction carries a theorem proving adherence to interface specs and 'the runtime system checks the theorem before' the transaction is allowed to take effect. This is runtime verification that prevents rather than merely detects, directly contradicting the bloom framing (echoed from the RV survey 'A survey of challenges for runtime verification from advanced application domains' 2019 and 'Runtime Verification of Ethereum Smart Contracts' 2018) that runtime monitoring is inherently post-hoc. 'Runtime Assertion Checking and Static Verification: Collaborative Partners' (2018) likewise treats the boundary as collaborative, not a detect-vs-prevent wall. If a pre-commit revert is the mechanism, bloom is already preventing, and the ADR's appeal to 'detection ≠ prevention' is rhetorical rather than load-bearing; if it is not pre-commit, TCT shows the strictly stronger primitive (carry-the-theorem) was available and ADR-002 picked the weaker one.
supports_if: Examples are found where bloom's view-function invariant runs post-commit (block-level or asynchronous) so a violating state is reachable before reversion, AND a TCT-style per-transaction theorem check would have closed that window — showing the chosen primitive is the weaker of two known options.
refutes_if: bloom's invariant is evaluated synchronously pre-commit such that any violating transaction reverts atomically, making it preventive in exactly the TCT sense — in which case the ADR's own 'detection ≠ prevention' justification is shown to be inapplicable to its own design (still a refutation of the stated rationale, not the mechanism) — OR TCT's per-transaction theorem overhead is shown to be infeasible at bloom's throughput.
motivating_papers: Theorem-Carrying Transactions: Runtime Verification to Ensure Interface Specifications for Smart Contract Safety
Runtime Assertion Checking and Static Verification: Collaborative Partners
A survey of challenges for runtime verification from advanced application domains (beyond software)

hypothesis: ADR-001 is built on a false impossibility claim: opaque closures and rich first-class predicates CAN be modularly specified and machine-checked, so forcing invariants into a 'restricted readable AST' needlessly amputates expressiveness that real DeFi invariants require, and the arbitration argument confuses 'opaque to a naive reader' with 'unverifiable'.
rationale: 'Modular specification and verification of closures in Rust' (2021) presents a technique that verifies rich functional properties of closures — including those that mutate captured state — by encoding higher-order concerns into first-order logic dischargeable by SMT, implemented in Prusti. That is a direct, peer-reviewed counterexample to ADR-001's 'opaque closures can't be arbitrated.' 'Flux: Liquid Types for Rust' (2022) and 'Verus: Verifying Rust Programs using Linear Ghost Types' (2023) further show that expressive, refinement/ghost-state predicates over arbitrary Rust are tractable. Meanwhile the industrial spec languages bloom imitates are deliberately expressive (quantifiers, ghost state) — 'Rich Specifications for Ethereum Smart Contract Verification' (2021) and 'The Move Prover' (2020) — suggesting that a 'restricted readable AST' risks being too weak to express the cross-function and temporal invariants real protocols need ('VerX'-style safety properties; 'Coalition Logic for Specification and Verification of Smart Contract Upgrades' 2022). The arbitration motive conflates human readability with adjudicability: a closure verified by a checker is adjudicable by replaying the checker, exactly as a restricted AST is.
supports_if: Concrete DeFi invariants (e.g., path-dependent / quantified / higher-order accumulator properties) are found in the corpus that the restricted-AST grammar cannot express but that closure/refinement verification (Prusti closures, Flux, Verus) can, AND a checker-replay adjudication scheme is shown to work for those richer predicates.
refutes_if: Evidence shows the restricted AST can express every invariant class the corpus identifies as security-relevant for DeFi, OR that closure/refinement verification of the kind in the cited papers is not reproducible across independent provers (and thus genuinely non-adjudicable in an adversarial setting), vindicating the restriction.
motivating_papers: Modular specification and verification of closures in Rust
Rich Specifications for Ethereum Smart Contract Verification

hypothesis: ADR-004's exclusion of floats 'because they are necessary for determinism and provability' solves a non-problem and may even be net-negative: typed/fixed-point Wasm subsets already deliver deterministic, verifiable arithmetic without banning a type, so the real determinism risk lies elsewhere (non-float nondeterminism, conformance gaps), and a blanket float ban buys little while the literature shows floats can be made consistent and certified.
rationale: 'CT-wasm: type-driven secure cryptography for the web ecosystem' (2019) and 'Formally Verified Cryptographic Web Applications in WebAssembly' (2019) show that disciplined, typed Wasm subsets give deterministic, machine-verified numeric behavior — i.e., determinism is achievable by typing/subsetting the operations actually used, not by excluding a whole numeric class. 'When Does a Bit Matter? Techniques for Verifying the Correctness of Assembly Languages and Floating-Point Programs' (2021), 'Floating-point–consistent cross-verification methodology...' (2026), and 'Lipschitz-Based Robustness Certification Under Floating-Point Execution' (2026) demonstrate that floating-point can be made reproducible and formally certified, so 'provability requires excluding floats' overstates the obstacle. Critically, the strongest empirical anchor, 'Detecting nondeterministic payment bugs in Ethereum smart contracts' (2019), locates consensus-breaking nondeterminism in system/ordering/state factors — Ethereum never had floats yet still had nondeterministic payment bugs — implying that banning floats addresses a minor surface while the dominant nondeterminism sources remain. The ban therefore risks misallocated effort and reduced expressiveness for legitimate fixed-point-unfriendly computations.
supports_if: The corpus's documented Wasm/blockchain nondeterminism and consensus bugs are overwhelmingly attributable to non-float causes (ordering, host calls, undefined-behavior, resource limits) per 'Detecting nondeterministic payment bugs...', AND IEEE-754 determinism under a pinned rounding mode / verified semantics is shown achievable (CT-wasm, the floating-point certification papers), making the categorical ban unnecessary.
refutes_if: Evidence shows that Wasm float semantics (NaN payloads, rounding, fast-math, SIMD) are genuinely under-specified or implementation-divergent in ways that no profile or typing discipline in the corpus can pin down deterministically, making exclusion the only sound option as ADR-004 claims.
motivating_papers: CT-wasm: type-driven secure cryptography for the web ecosystem
Detecting nondeterministic payment bugs in Ethereum smart contracts
When Does a Bit Matter? Techniques for Verifying the Correctness of Assembly Languages and Floating-Point Programs

hypothesis: ADR-005 has it backwards: pinning a conformance PROFILE plus test vectors instead of a binary is insufficient for a consensus-critical VM, because test-vector conformance under-determines execution semantics on adversarial inputs; soundness here requires pinning a verified executable semantics (or a single canonical binary), and the profile-not-binary choice reintroduces exactly the implementation-divergence nondeterminism it claims to prevent.
rationale: 'Mechanising and verifying the WebAssembly specification' (WasmCert, 2018) and 'WasmRef-Isabelle: A Verified Monadic Interpreter and Industrial Fuzzing Oracle for WebAssembly' (2023) succeed precisely by pinning a complete mechanized SEMANTICS, not a finite test suite — and WasmRef-Isabelle is used as a fuzzing oracle exactly because conformance test suites miss cases. 'Wasm SpecTec: Engineering a Formal Language Standard' (2023) notes that even the official process couples a formal spec, prose, reference interpreter, AND tests because no single artifact (least of all the test suite) fully pins behavior. 'Uncovering Smart Contract VM Bugs Via Differential Fuzzing' (2021) and 'Detecting nondeterministic payment bugs in Ethereum smart contracts' (2019) empirically show conformant-looking VMs diverging on untested inputs — the precise failure mode a test-vector profile cannot foreclose in a consensus setting. Since bloom needs bit-identical replay for fraud proofs (ADR-007), a profile that admits multiple semantically inequivalent implementations is a latent consensus fork.
supports_if: The corpus yields cases of VMs/Wasm engines passing a conformance/test-vector suite yet diverging on adversarial or under-tested inputs (differential fuzzing results, WasmRef-Isabelle oracle catches), demonstrating that a profile + vectors does not uniquely determine execution and a pinned semantics/binary would have.
refutes_if: Evidence shows a conformance profile plus a sufficiently rich vector suite is provably equivalent to pinning a semantics for the deterministic subset bloom uses (e.g., SpecTec-generated exhaustive tests), so binary pinning would add no soundness and only add brittleness — vindicating ADR-005.
motivating_papers: WasmRef-Isabelle: A Verified Monadic Interpreter and Industrial Fuzzing Oracle for WebAssembly
Uncovering Smart Contract VM Bugs Via Differential Fuzzing
Wasm SpecTec: Engineering a Formal Language Standard

hypothesis: ADR-007's re-execution / fraud-proof fallback is not a sound backstop for zkVM underconstraint but a category error: a soundness bug (the prover accepting an invalid execution) cannot be caught by honest re-execution because both the malicious prover and the honest re-executor can agree on the same wrong-but-accepted result, so bloom's 'no single prover + re-execute' design fails against exactly the failure class it cites, and the real fix is prover-circuit verification or differential proving, not replay.
rationale: 'Arguzz: Testing zkVMs for Soundness and Completeness Bugs' (2025) defines soundness bugs as the zkVM 'accepting invalid executions' arising from bugs in the constraint system, and detects them via metamorphic testing + fault injection — not via re-execution. A fraud-proof/re-execution fallback assumes the honest re-execution and the proof disagree; but an underconstrained circuit accepts a forged trace whose claimed output the re-executor, running the SAME unsound semantics or honestly reproducing the attacker's chosen inputs, may not flag as fraudulent. 'Formal Verification of Zero-Knowledge Circuits' (2023) and 'Towards Fuzzing Zero-Knowledge Proof Circuits' (2025) locate the defense at the CIRCUIT level (proving the constraint system is fully constrained), implying ADR-007's protocol-level replay is solving the wrong layer. 'The Autopoiesis of Verifiable Computation: Analyzing the Nexus zkVM...' (2025) and 'Evaluating Compiler Optimization Impacts on zkVM Performance' (2025) further suggest zkVM trust must be established intrinsically (verified constraints, toolchain), not via an external re-run.
supports_if: The corpus shows underconstraint/soundness bugs (Arguzz, ZK-circuit fuzzing) whose forged executions would be ACCEPTED by an honest re-executor or produce no detectable fraud signal at the protocol layer — demonstrating re-execution cannot distinguish a soundness-broken proof from a valid one.
refutes_if: Evidence shows that for bloom's execution model, every underconstraint-accepted trace necessarily diverges from honest re-execution on a checkable public output (so a fraud proof always exists and is constructible), making re-execution a complete backstop and circuit-level verification merely an optimization.
motivating_papers: Arguzz: Testing zkVMs for Soundness and Completeness Bugs
Towards Fuzzing Zero-Knowledge Proof Circuits (Short Paper)
